articles.title: Always tired? Leaving your ‘loops’ open may be the unexpected cause
articles.summary: Procrastinating on some tasks may feel harmless, but the perpetual mental hum of unfinished business may cause more stress than you realize.
articles.body:
The texts you've ignored, the vacation supplies you still need to order, the hard conversation you've been avoiding — repeatedly putting off such tasks because they feel too daunting may seem relatively harmless. But the constant mental hum of unfinished business may be more draining than you realize — like your laptop slowing and glitching because you have 90 browser tabs open.

Some people are waking up to that reality, sharing on social media and in podcasts their epiphanies about the countless open "loops" in their lives in need of closing. The buzzy phrase helps them more easily recognize and combat the habit.

As New Yorker Florence Friebe learned about open loops, she began to see the pattern in her own life — for example, via a hole in her jacket pocket that she kept neglecting to fix and remembered every time she dropped her keys or phone into it.

"I could really start seeing how many repetitive thoughts I was carrying, and how much space it was taking," added Friebe, cohost of the podcast "2 Curly Haired Girls With ADHD" — referring not only to the effects of procrastinating on fixing her jacket pocket but also on cleaning and work tasks.

Psychologists who study procrastination say these people are right to address these issues.

The inertia comes from perceiving "the 'cost' of doing the task in terms of time, energy, and emotional fatigue," said Dr. Vara Saripalli, a clinical psychologist in private practice in Chicago, via email. "They aren't thinking about the other negatives that ensue from waiting; they're focused on the present and avoiding unpleasantness in the here and now."

But as Friebe learned, avoidance also can be highly costly, both practically and by taking up energy that could be used for other things, Saripalli added.

Procrastination and chronic stress can eventually take a toll on both your mental and physical health, said Dr. Fuschia Sirois, professor of social and health psychology at Durham University in England. Sirois, a procrastination expert who has been studying the issue for 25 years, is also the author of "Procrastination: What It Is, Why It's a Problem, and What You Can Do About It."

Those impacts include causing or contributing to a weakened immune system, chronic disease, anxiety and digestive issues, low self-esteem and loneliness, Sirois added.

For Lanna, a content creator and Pilates instructor in Germany, procrastination-related worries even caused stomachaches, she said. Lanna requested that CNN use her nickname for privacy.

But for many people, awareness of these impacts doesn't always make taking action easier.

For generally healthy people, habitual procrastination typically boils down to two causes, even if the details differ per individual, experts said: negative emotions associated with certain tasks or with the prospect of those tasks not going well.

Maybe you're delaying replying to a text because you haven't figured out a perfect response, and you have complicated feelings around imperfection. Or maybe you're avoiding a serious talk with a friend because you're people-pleasing or worried you'll be hurt. (You can read more about procrastination "styles" and related tips here .)

Procrastinating on relatively minor things sometimes may stem from a broader societal shift Saripalli has noticed, in which people are less comfortable with finality and losing options, she said. "The simple task of returning a package becomes an internal monologue of, 'What if I change my mind and I can't get this item again? I'm better off holding on to it till I'm sure.'"

On the other hand, you may just have too many responsibilities and need to consider which ones you can forgo. Maybe you're exhausted by other commitments or spending too much time on your phone, which can be a distraction and energy zapper.

Or maybe the cause of your procrastination is more complicated. If you're struggling to overcome procrastination on your own, consider seeing a doctor or therapist to determine whether there's a more serious underlying issue, Sirois said — such as depression, ADHD or an anxiety disorder.

These disorders can make one's tolerance of negative feelings about a task much lower, Sirois added. That, as well as other symptoms, can contribute to people with these disorders being more prone to procrastinate.

In those cases, some coping strategies can help, but they don't cure disorders or replace professional assistance, Sirois said.

That was true for Lanna, who said she has ADHD and autism, and for Friebe. Friebe said she realized that her struggles with procrastination were significantly tied to her ADHD, depression and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome , or PMOS.

"It was almost like I was lacking ingredients," Friebe said. "Once I got diagnosed, it felt like a giant relief."

Awareness of your urges to procrastinate and of the likely consequences can sometimes be enough to help you regulate your emotions, then choose differently.

But some people such as Friebe and Lanna have also sought professional help for their conditions and improved their lifestyle habits. These changes have given them more energy and the confidence to be more efficient.

Seeing a therapist can really be helpful for anyone regardless of whether you have a condition since they can help you deal with pessimistic ideas causing procrastination. Sirois recently released a free, online evidence-based tool kit for that purpose.

Now Friebe schedules free time to tackle whatever tasks she's got at the moment. Doing a job little by little — or styling to-do list tasks that way — has been more effective than anticipating it with the all-or-nothing thinking that can make responsibilities feel daunting. What also helps Lanna is doing activities that rejuvenate her.

And Friebe really means little , even if that feels stupid, she said. She referred to a story she heard of people who wanted to start exercising at a gym driving to the gym, as they were, on the days they had said they wanted to work out — but not going inside.

The next time, those people also put on workout clothes before driving. Next, they went to the gym in their outfits and exercised for only five minutes. "What they were actually building was trust that they were reliable, that they could do it, so then it could accumulate," Friebe said. "Before you knew it, they were working out."

Studies support the effectiveness of such gradual habit-building.

Guilt and shame are the two most common emotions people feel when they procrastinate, Sirois said, which compound the problem and further paralyze you — even though taking action would alleviate all those negative feelings. "Being self-compassionate is actually a more effective way to get oneself back on track," she added.

Acknowledge that you're struggling and what you're feeling, and ask yourself whether the situation at hand will really be that bad. "Often, we anticipate things are going to be much worse than what they are," Sirois said. Even if your attempts don't go well, trust that you can learn how to navigate the fallout and be OK.

Also try to find the meaning in different responsibilities, those interviewed recommended. If you're delaying cleaning your room and beating yourself up about whether your roommate is judging you for the mess, think about the fact that you deserve a clean, cozy space.

Friebe and Lanna consider how productivity might bring them closer to their life purpose or the person they want to be. And if a heart-to-heart goes poorly, even then, the meaning can be that you grew in your ability to handle conflict, and that you have the truth about the relationship and can act accordingly.

If you're avoiding scheduling a doctor's appointment because you don't want to hear their feedback, your health issue exists regardless. So why not get some answers and prevent your problem from worsening? Regardless of the task, think of how relaxed you'll feel and how much time you'll free up for other fun things if you just get it done.

Since Friebe has improved her health and learned what strategies work for her, "the way I speak to myself is completely different," she said.

"I have a better sense of self and identity and self-trust," Friebe added. "My entire life has changed. I'm a different person."

articles.title: Algeria’s schools put Shakespeare before Molière in break from France
articles.summary: Algerian primary schools will begin teaching English before French for the first time, signalling a drift from France.
articles.body:
Ahmed Krim spent 30 years teaching English in Algeria’s middle schools. Now retired, the 60-year-old watched the language he loved remain firmly behind French as the country’s second language.

English was less valued than French, which might have been the language of Algeria’s coloniser, but continues to be present in every dialogue, six decades after independence.

On July 25 , Algeria’s Education Minister, Mohamed Seghir Saadaoui, announced that English will become the sole foreign language taught in the third year of primary school in the new academic year for 2026-2027.

French would be pushed back to the fourth year, ending its domination of foreign language classes in Algerian schools.

From next month, eight-year-olds across Algeria will become the first to learn English before French.

“It is a very good decision. But it requires thinking, planning and resources,” Krim told Al Jazeera.

It is among the first steps in President Abdelmadjid Tebboune’s linguistic overhaul for Algeria, which he first outlined in 2022 with English being introduced to primary schools.

Since then, medicine and science faculties have begun switching from French to English.

The French language has been erased from some utility bills and Air Algerie tickets. Road signs are beginning to feature English alongside Arabic, while government ministers’ websites will also have English as an option.

The shift from French to English as Algeria’s secondary language is both sweeping and structural.

It comes amid the most serious diplomatic crisis between the two countries since Algeria’s independence from France in 1962.

In July 2024, French President Emmanuel Macron publicly backed Morocco’s sovereignty claim over Western Sahara.

Algeria, which supports the Sahrawi Polisario Front and hosts over 170,000 Sahrawi refugees, viewed that as highly provocative.

That, and other issues, saw Algeria expel French diplomats , and vice versa.

Algeria’s replacement of French as the country’s second language accelerated after the diplomatic crisis grew.

A rethink of the whole education system in Algeria may be needed.

“First and foremost, specialised training centres must be restored and candidates must not be forced into the teaching profession without wanting it – we need people who genuinely want to do this work,” Krim said.

He refers to dedicated institutes established after independence, where primary and middle school teachers, like himself, trained via a model that combined classroom instruction with direct school placements to meet the gap in Arabic instructors.

The centres operated until the late 1990s, when an economic crunch replaced them with the fewer and more selective Ecoles Normales Superieures.

Most teachers today are university graduates, but lack the practical, classroom-first grounding that the older model provided.

Krim said that school curricula must be designed and entrusted to “a qualified body that includes both linguistic and pedagogical expertise, free from all ideology”.

But journalist and analyst Noureddine Bessadi said the ideological dimension matters in Algeria, which overthrew colonialism following a bloody and bitter struggle against the French.

“Since independence in 1962, every shift in language policy has been fought as much on political as pedagogical grounds,” Bessadi told Al Jazeera.

After independence, Algeria’s Arabisation drive, when French was displaced from government and education, was “part of state building and enforcing Algeria’s identity, centring Arabic and Islam”, Bessadi added.

Tamazight, a non-Semitic language spoken by around a quarter of Algeria’s population, was marginalised until 1995, Bessadi said, shaped by an “ideological perception of unity that prioritised linguistic and cultural harmony”.

Critics argue that the transition from French to English is happening faster than the system can keep up with. For one, it is believed that there are not enough qualified English teachers to make the language reforms work.

But one source familiar with the matter told Al Jazeera that there are enough teachers to roll out this programme in primary schools and that any shortage could be filled through contractors.

In February, Algeria’s education ministry reportedly recruited about 15,000 English language teachers for primary schools.

Rafik Laceb, a lecturer in English at Mouloud Mammeri University in Tizi Ouzou, is cautiously optimistic about the primary school reform. But he considers the parallel push to teach university subjects in English to be rushed and poorly executed.

“Frankly, and beyond any chauvinism, I believe this decision is positive… I believe there is, today, sufficient supervision and evaluation work from the first experience,” Laceb said, in reference to the previous introduction of English in later primary school years.

The university experiment that began in 2023-2024 produced insufficient contact hours, a lack of genuine assessment of students’ English levels and no tracking of their progress.

Around 50 percent of teaching at Tizi Ouzou University’s English department is by younger contract staff, which brings other challenges.

“A young contract teacher must first master the basic principles of medicine before attempting to teach medical terminology in English,” he said.

Currently, children only begin learning a foreign language in the third year of state primary schools, whereas multiple languages are taught at private schools from kindergarten.

Djamel Merah, whose daughter attended private schools before transferring to public secondary school, studied Arabic, French and English simultaneously from kindergarten level.

Merah welcomes the government’s language reforms at state primary schools, which will provide more children with the opportunity to learn English.

“It addresses a question about the gap in opportunities between children who get multilingual education from the start and those in public schools who don’t get the same chance,” he said.

There also appears to be a more organic response among the public that precedes the government’s promotion of the English language.

Krimo Taleb, a bookseller at the Libre Pensee bookshop in Tizi Ouzou, has seen a growth in English-language book sales, particularly among female readers.

“In my opinion, it has nothing to do with government decisions. The majority of young readers today speak three languages fluently,” he said.

His own daughter, a middle school student, reads fluently in Arabic, English and French.

Colleen Hoover, Ana Huang and J. K. Rowling are some of the best-selling authors at his shop.

“Previously, our bookshops provided for English literature students the works of Shakespeare,” Taleb says. “Today, there is a diverse range of English-language titles aimed at the general public.”

However, French remains Algeria’s most influential foreign language. According to the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF), Algeria has approximately 15 million French speakers, nearly a third of its population.

There is not a single newspaper published in English and written English by Algerians remains in its infancy.

But there are signs that former colonies are turning their backs on France’s linguistic legacy, particularly in Africa, where Paris’s military and political presence made a resurgence in recent decades .

In March 2025, Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso withdrew from the OIF, accusing it of being a political instrument of Paris.

“Mali made its national languages official in 2023, demoting French to a working language. Burkina Faso followed the same year and Niger in 2025,” Bessadi added. “Even Senegal, which has not removed French as an official language, has begun encouraging local languages at its expense.”

For Krim, Algeria’s linguistic ambitions are not far-fetched, but for it to work, the country needs the “necessary resources… and transparency”.

articles.title: In 1998, Costa Rica spread 12,000 tonnes of orange waste over degraded pasture; 16 years later, tree diversity had tripled and forest biomass was 176% higher
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In the late 1990s, an unusual conservation experiment began in Costa Rica when ecologists proposed using orange peels and pulp to help restore a badly.
articles.body: In the late 1990s, an unusual conservation experiment began in Costa Rica when ecologists proposed using orange peels and pulp to help restore a badly degraded piece of land inside a national park.For this, orange juice company Del Oro and ecologists Daniel Janzen and Winnie Hallwachs, worked with the Area de Conservacion Guanacaste (ACG), or Guanacaste Conservation Area. According to Princeton University, the company had recently started production near the northern border of the conservation area and was looking for a way to deal with its orange waste.Janzen and Hallwachs proposed a deal wherein Del Oro would donate some of its forested land to the ACG. In return, the company could take its orange peel waste to a degraded pasture inside the park, where it could break down naturally.After the agreement was signed, around 1,000 truckloads of orange peels and pulp, totalling about 12,000 metric tonnes, were spread across the degraded land.Over the next several years, the area changed dramatically. A place that had once been covered by exposed rock and dead grass became a dense forest filled with trees, vines and other vegetation.A forest emergesThe site was largely forgotten after the orange waste was deposited. A rival orange juice company, TicoFruit, later sued Del Oro, arguing that the company had defiled a national park. The case reached Costa Ricaâs Supreme Court, which ruled in favour of TicoFruit.The legal dispute meant that the site received little attention for about 15 years. That changed in 2013, when Princeton University researcher Timothy Treuer was discussing possible research projects with Janzen.Janzen mentioned the orange-peel site to Treuer and said that although taxonomists had visited the area, it had not received a thorough evaluation. Treuer decided to visit it during another research trip to Costa Rica.When he arrived, the site looked completely different from what he expected. The vegetation had grown so densely that Treuer could not initially see the large sign marking the experiment.âIt was so completely overgrown with trees and vines that I couldnât even see the 7-foot-long sign with bright yellow lettering marking the site that was only a few feet from the road,â Treuer said, as quoted by Princeton.The contrast became even clearer when Treuer compared the orange-peel site with the nearby untreated pasture. The treated area had become a thick forest, while the neighbouring land remained much more open.âIt was just hard to believe that the only difference between the two areas was a bunch of orange peels. They look like completely different ecosystems,â Treuer explained.Researchers assess forestTreuer worked with Jonathan Choi, then a Princeton student studying ecology and evolutionary biology. The researchers compared the area treated with orange waste with a nearby untreated pasture. They also collected and analysed soil samples from both sites to determine whether the orange waste had changed the soil over time.They also measured vegetation in both areas. The team established 100-metre-long lines, known as transects, through the forest. Trees growing within three metres of these lines were measured and identified. The same approach was used in the untreated pasture across the road.The differences were substantial. The soil in the orange-waste area was richer in nutrients. The area also had greater tree biomass, more tree species and a more closed forest canopy.The study found a 176% increase in aboveground biomass within the three-hectare area that was examined. Aboveground biomass refers to the wood and other plant material growing above the soil, including the trees.The researchers also found a major difference in tree diversity. While the surrounding areas were dominated by one type of tree, the former orange-waste site had about two dozen species of vegetation.Wildlife returned to restored areaThe changes were not limited to plants. Researchers also found signs of a more developed ecosystem at the site. Among the discoveries was a tayra, a dog-sized mammal related to weasels, Diario AS reported. The researchers also found a huge fig tree that had grown in the area.Jonathan Choi described the site as even more impressive in person than he had expected. âWhile I would walk over exposed rock and dead grass in the nearby fields, Iâd have to climb through undergrowth and cut paths through walls of vines in the orange peel site itself.âThe size of the fig tree was another indication of how much the area had changed. Choi said the tree was about three feet in diameter and described it as massive. âYou could have had 20 people climbing in that tree at once and it would have supported the weight no problem. That thing was massive,â he said.The researchers published their findings in the journal Restoration Ecology in a paper titled âLow-Cost Agricultural Waste Accelerates Tropical Forest Regenerationâ.Timothy Treuer said the experiment was unusual because it showed that forest restoration and waste management could potentially work together. âThis is one of the only instances Iâve ever heard of where you can have cost-negative carbon sequestration,â Treuer said. âItâs not just a win-win between the company and the local park; itâs a win for everyone.âThe researchers, however, did not suggest that companies should simply take their waste and dump it in natural areas. Treuer specifically warned against such an approach. âWe donât want companies to go out there willy-nilly just dumping their waste all over the place,â Treuer said. âBut if itâs scientifically driven and restorationists are involved in addition to companies, this is something I think has really high potential.âCatch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Nigeria drug arrests: '101-year-old great-grandmother' detained for selling cannabis
articles.summary: Esther Ogunmabo is accused of selling "retail sachets" of a strain of cannabis known as skunk.
articles.body:
An elderly woman, who the authorities say is 101, has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly selling cannabis, in a case that has drawn widespread attention.

Esther Ogunmabo, described as a great-grandmother, was apprehended on Saturday in Ogun state, in the south-west of the country, the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) announced.

Femi Babafemi, the agency's media director, said the centenarian was found with "retail sachets of skunk, a strain of cannabis weighing 90 grams, which she claims she sells to locals".

The NDLEA said the suspect told investigators that she turned to the illicit drug trade after her provisions shop was destroyed by fire. She has been released on bail.

According to the Ndlea, one of her daughters, who lives in Lagos, allegedly arranged for the supply of the substance to her every four days. Ogunmabo is accused of then selling it on in smaller quantities to customers in her community.

Ndlea chief executive Mohamed Marwa directed that the suspect be granted bail and given counselling because of her advanced age.

Ogunmabo’s bail status means she could still be charged for criminal activity.

Ogunmabo’s arrest came as the Ndlea also reported significant drug seizures along Nigeria's maritime routes.

In Akwa Ibom state, operatives acting on credible intelligence intercepted a wooden boat on the high seas last Friday, which was heading to Cameroon, and arrested three people on board.

More than 42kg of narcotics were recovered from the suspects.

In what the agency described as a milestone, the Ndlea also recorded its first-ever seizure of illicit drugs shipped from Thailand.

articles.title: Israel warns of 'forceful' response to kites flown from Gaza
articles.summary: Hamas says the kites found in Israeli border communities in recent days were launched by children in Gaza.
articles.body:
Israel has warned Hamas that it will increase strikes on Gaza following concern over launches of kites, drones and balloons from the territory.

Several kites were found in an Israeli community near the border with Gaza over the weekend, local media reported.

"Forceful actions will be taken to put an end to this phenomenon," Israel's Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Monday.

Before the war, kites and balloons carrying incendiary devices were launched into Israel, causing fires that burned forest and farmland.

Hamas has denied responsibility for the new kites - which were not carrying explosives - and said they belonged to "children searching for their innocent childhood amid the rubble".

The group also accused Israel of using the kites as a "pretext" for continued air strikes in Gaza despite the ceasefire agreed last October.

UK, Canada and Australia condemn Israel for refusing criminal probe into aid worker killings in Gaza Published 4 days ago

UK, Canada and Australia condemn Israel for refusing criminal probe into aid worker killings in Gaza

Israel confirms soldiers fired at car in which Hind Rajab was killed and opens criminal investigation Published 5 days ago

Israel confirms soldiers fired at car in which Hind Rajab was killed and opens criminal investigation

Families' agonising search for answers as thousands still missing in Gaza Published 6 days ago

Families' agonising search for answers as thousands still missing in Gaza

Four kites were found in Kibbutz Nahal Oz, which is about 800m (2,620ft) from the Gaza border, on Friday and Saturday. Several more were found elsewhere in southern Israel last week, according to local media.

The Israeli reports cited military sources as saying they believed Hamas was behind the kites and that they might have been intended to test Israel's response.

No suspicious materials were attached to the kites and they did not pose a threat, the military said.

But Katz warned there would be "zero tolerance" and said: "A balloon is treated like a kite, and a kite is treated like a drone, with or without explosives."

Residents of Nahal Oz said in a statement that they feared the return of incendiary kites and balloons, adding: "We will not accept a policy of containment when it comes to our security."

Hamas warned of "the danger of the allegations and threats" from Israel and said the kites were "basically children's toys from displacement camps".

"These threats are based on fabricated pretexts and are an attempt to justify the continuation of the aggression and violations against our people," a spokesman for the group added.

On Sunday, Palestinian health officials said two people were killed and seven others injured in two Israeli strikes in Nuseirat refugee camp and the town of al-Zawayda, both in central Gaza.

A four-year-old boy called Mohammed Taha was killed when a building in al-Zawayda, just north of Maghazi refugee camp, was bombed, according to local media.

The Israeli military said it killed the commander of a Hamas weapons manufacturing site in the Maghazi area, whom it identified as Ismail Abu Ful, and that it had warned the residents to evacuate beforehand.

"There is no ceasefire, there is nothing," Abu Ahmed, a displaced man who had been sheltering nearby, told Reuters news agency. "We want solutions, we want to live in peace."

On Monday, Palestinian media reported that a man called Mohammed Abu Asad was killed in an overnight Israeli strike on a tent in the central town of Deir al-Balah.

The Israeli military said Abu Asad was a member of the elite Nukhba forces of Hamas's military wing who had taken part in the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attack on southern Israel.

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to the cross-border assault, during which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

More than 74,420 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since then, including 1,288 since the ceasefire took effect, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry.

articles.title: 'Their faces burnt': Disturbing details emerge in Bangladesh Hindu family murder
articles.summary: South Asia News: A Hindu family of four was found murdered inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city, with investigators uncovering disturbing details abou.
articles.body: A Hindu family of four was found murdered inside their locked home in Bangladeshâs Rangpur city, with investigators uncovering disturbing details about the killings and an alleged attempt to destroy evidence.The victims were identified as retired Rangpur Zilla School teacher Ganapati Chakraborty, 65, his wife Pritilata Chakraborty, 50, their 23-year-old daughter Agami Chakraborty Prarthi and their 12-year-old son Priyam Chakraborty. Their bodies were recovered from their home in the Daspara (Machhuapara) area at around 11.30pm on Saturday.According to Bangladeshâs The Daily Star, Pritilataâs younger sister Puja Chakraborty said the family noticed that the victimsâ faces had been burnt when the bodies were handed over to them.âWhen we received the bodies in the evening, we found that their faces had been burned. Earlier, police did not allow us to go near the bodies,â Puja said.Sumit Chowdhury, acting superintendent of police of CID Rangpur, told The Daily Star that investigators suspected a flammable substance had been used on the victimsâ faces.âThe killers appear to have poured a flammable substance on the victimsâ faces either before or after killing them. At this stage, we cannot say what substance was used. The investigating officer will collect samples and send them to the CID forensic department for examination. We will know more once the test results are available.âThe bodies were found in different parts of the house. The mother and daughter were found on the staircase, Ganapatiâs body was recovered from the roof, while Priyam was found under a bed. Police initially suspected that the family had been strangled, with the killings believed to have taken place between midnight on Thursday and early Friday.Investigators said suspects Mugdha and Siddhartha allegedly remained inside the house after the killings. According to Prothom Alo, they reportedly bathed there, ate dates and cucumbers from the refrigerator and used yaba before leaving on Friday during Jummah prayers, when the streets were relatively quiet.Police also found cupboards and drawers opened and belongings scattered, suggesting an attempt to make the killings appear to be a robbery. Evidence allegedly indicated an attempt to test a gold bangle using fire, while two phones belonging to the victims had been submerged in water mixed with detergent, apparently to destroy evidence.The suspects were detained based on these clues and allegedly confessed during questioning, police said. Gold jewellery believed to have been stolen was later recovered from an abandoned location they identified. Date pits found inside the house have also been sent for DNA testing, according to Prothom Alo.Puja said the family had not been heard from since Thursday and all four phones were switched off. Police later broke open the locked main gate and found the bodies.Police, CID and Detective Branch teams are jointly investigating the case, while preparations were under way to file a murder case.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Shelley Fabares, ‘Johnny Angel’ singer and actor on ‘The Donna Reed Show’ and ‘Coach,’ dies at 82
articles.summary: Fabares died Saturday in Los Angeles, her family said. No cause was given.
articles.body: Shelley Fabares, an actor who was a fixture on television for decades from her days as a young teenager on “The Donna Reed Show,” through “One Day at a Time” and “Coach,” has died. She was 82. She died Saturday in Los Angeles, her family said in a statement to The Associated Press. No cause was given. “To her family and friends, Shelley was a source of love, strength, laughter, and comfort,” her family wrote. “She had a remarkable ability to make people feel welcomed, valued, and cared for.” Fabares was born in Santa Monica, California, in 1944, and started acting as a young child. Her first television credit came at age 10 when she appeared on “The Loretta Young Show.” Many movies and television shows followed: She acted with Paul Newman, Frank Sinatra and Eva Marie Saint in a Producers Showcase production of “Our Town” and was in the Rosalind Russell movie “The Girl Rush” and the Rock Hudson drama “Never Say Goodbye.” Other early credits include “Annette,” “Captain Midnight” and the “Black Leather Jackets” episode of “The Twilight Zone.” Her biggest break came when she was cast as Mary Stone on “The Donna Reed Show,” where she was a regular from 1958 through 1963. During that time she also got a recording contract and had two Top 40 hits, including “Johnny Angel.” In the early 1960s, she also co-starred in three movies with Elvis Presley: “Girl Happy,” “Spinout” and “Clambake.” “I think the years on ‘The Donna Reed Show,’ the years from 14 to 19, were so incredibly important,” Fabares told the Los Angeles Times in 1993. “Donna Reed was simply an extraordinary woman, a woman of great strength, kindness, integrity and compassion. I am not trying to make her sound like a saint, but she had the most profound influence on me. I carry her with me today.” In the late 1970s, Fabares made an impression as Francine Webster on the CBS sitcom “One Day at a Time.” She also played James Caan’s wife in “Brian’s Song.” One of her biggest roles came when she was cast as Christine Armstrong in “Coach,” although the show took a minute to find its audience. “I did always feel from the very beginning if they could find the right spot for us, this was a show that would last,” she said in the 1993 Los Angeles Times interview. Fabares married twice, first to producer Lou Adler in 1964. She had been married to “M-A-S-H” actor Mike Farrell since 1984. She was also a devoted advocate for Alzheimer’s awareness, which affected her mother. In early 1999, a visit to the emergency room for an esophageal bleed revealed that she had progressive liver failure. After spending 22 months on a waiting list, she had liver transplant surgery in October 2000. In an interview with Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles three years after the transplant, she said she’d been “changed by the experience” and was eternally grateful to Farrell, who was with her “every step of the way.” Her family, in their statement, said that “we will remember Shelley for her kindness, loyalty, wit, courage, and beautiful spirit. We will miss her deeply — not only as a celebrated performer, but as the loving and extraordinary person she was in our everyday lives.”

articles.title: Royal Shakespeare Company backs plan for £600m theme park near Bicester
articles.summary: A company submitted a planning application for the attraction in the Oxfordshire countryside last year.
articles.body:
The Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) has backed plans to build a £600m history-based theme park in the Oxfordshire countryside.

French firm Puy du Fou submitted proposals to build the site, north of Bicester, to Cherwell District Council last year.

The RSC described the proposal as an "exciting opportunity to further enhance the UK's cultural and tourism offer".

Puy du Fou has said it aims to open the park in phases, beginning in 2029 and that it would employ about 2,000 people. Its plans have sparked concerns from some locals, who have expressed fears about the impact the site will have on things such as traffic and wildlife.

A new group has also been created to bring together representatives from Heyford Park and surrounding villages to discuss the impact of major schemes planned in the area, including the theme park.

The forum, approved by Oxfordshire County Council, wants to help prevent the area from "descending into traffic gridlock".

But Blenheim Palace , national tourism agency VisitBritain , performing arts and entertainment trade union Equity , and Experience Oxfordshire, are among those who have previously backed the theme park plan.

The Puy du Fou attraction would include four period villages and 13 live shows in which visitors could "immerse themselves in British history".

Developers estimate the attraction could welcome up to 1.4 million visitors a year once fully open.

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

In a letter seen by the BBC, issued by the RSC's senior leadership team to the council, and confirmed by the organisation as authentic, it said: "We recognise the important role that major cultural and visitor attractions can play in strengthening the regional economy, increasing tourism, creating employment opportunities, and encouraging wider participation in arts, culture, and heritage.

"There is currently no equivalent attraction operating at this scale within the UK, and we can see the potential for the project to attract new visitors to the region, generate economic activity, and contribute to the continued growth of the visitor economy across the Midlands and surrounding areas."

The letter said the RSC was "particularly encouraged by the potential for collaboration across the cultural, tourism, hospitality, and education sectors".

"Major attractions often act as catalysts for wider partnerships, helping organisations work together to create richer visitor experiences and strengthen the overall appeal of a destination," it added.

The RSC concluded that it supported the "ambitions" of the project and the "potential benefits it could bring to the region, its communities, and the wider visitor economy".

Puy du Fou has had history-themed parks in Les Epesses in France since 1978 and in Toledo, Spain, since 2021.

articles.title: Washington Post ordered to reinstate columnist Karen Attiah after being terminated over Charlie Kirk posts
articles.summary: The Washington Post has been ordered to reinstate columnist Karen Attiah after being fired for Bluesky posts about Charlie Kirk's assassination.
articles.body: The Washington Post was ordered to reinstate columnist Karen Attiah after she was fired last year for social media posts she made after Charlie Kirk's assassination. Sarah Miller Espinosa, the arbitrator overseeing Attiah's legal challenge against The Post, said the paper "did not have good and sufficient cause" and that it "violated" her labor agreement, according to The New York Times, which first reported on Espinosa's ruling last Thursday. "The Washington Post failed to establish the grievant engaged in gross misconduct," Espinosa concluded. TEACHERS WHO CELEBRATED CHARLIE KIRK'S ASSASSINATION NOW CASH IN WITH TAXPAYER-FUNDED SETTLEMENTS Attiah told The Times she is "relieved to finally have that record set straight," adding, "This decision confirms what we’ve said from the start: I was doing my job as an opinion writer, and this was wrongful termination." The columnist announced her legal victory, saying on X, "The Washington Post fired me last year for speaking the truth after Charlie Kirk's killing. I fought back. I'm happy to announce: I won my case against the Washington Post. They have been ordered to reinstate me immediately." "In general, if someone reveals themselves to be a ghoul then companies should be able to fire them," Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet told Fox News Digital.  A spokesperson for The Washington Post said the paper respects the arbitration process and declined to comment further. Attiah didn't immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Attiah sparked outrage for her posts about the slain conservative icon on the liberal social media platform Bluesky. In a separate post, she wrote, "Part of what keeps America so violent is the insistence that people perform care, empty goodness and absolution for White men who espouse hatred and violence.’" Critics also slammed Attiah for misquoting Kirk in another post, attributing to him saying, "Black women do not have the brain processing power to be taken seriously. You have to go steal a White person's slot." On a July 2023 episode of "The Charlie Kirk Show," Kirk actually said, "If we would have said three weeks ago [...] that Joy Reid and Michelle Obama, and Sheila Jackson Lee, and Ketanji Brown Jackson were affirmative-action picks, we would have been called racist. But now they're comin' out and they're saying it for us! They're comin' out, and they're saying, 'I'm only here because of affirmative action.' Yeah, we know. You do not have the brain processing power to otherwise be taken really seriously. You had to go steal a White person's slot to go be taken somewhat seriously." Following the backlash, Attiah revealed she had been fired by The Post, saying in a termination letter her posts were "unacceptable" and "gross misconduct." articles.title: What should you wear through airport security? Frequent fliers recommend these fuss-free pieces
articles.summary: Consider this your cheat sheet for a smoother trip through TSA lines — not to mention a smoother trip overall.
articles.body:
Our experts independently review everything we recommend. If you buy through our links, we may earn commission.

Getting through airport security is stressful enough, so your outfit shouldn't be the thing holding up the line. Looking polished is always a plus, but the best travel outfits work smarter, not harder. Think easy-on, easy-off shoes , layers that don't require a full wardrobe change and clever pieces that keep you from frantically digging through your bag while everyone behind you silently judges.

So, what actually deserves a spot in your airport uniform? We asked frequent fliers to share their wardrobe standbys. From shoes made for breezing through security to fuss-free layers and smart, travel-friendly details, consider this your boarding pass for getting through the airport with less hassle — and more time for the important things, like finding your gate and grabbing a snack (or maybe a pre-flight glass of wine).

These things don't have to be on opposite sides of the terminal. The best travel outfits hit that sweet spot: Soft, stretchy and roomy enough to survive hours in a cramped seat, but polished enough that you won't be rushing to change the second you land. "I think comfort and style go hand in hand," says travel YouTuber Ally Gibson . "Comfort is non-negotiable, especially on long-haul flights. That said, you never know who you might meet, and looking good makes you feel good throughout the day."

Sometimes the secret to a comfortable travel outfit is less what you wear and more what you leave at home. "I avoid jeans, belts and anything tight because sitting in restrictive clothing becomes uncomfortable on a long travel day, especially when your body can feel more swollen during a flight," explains travel blogger Hazel McKinlay .

And while the days of dressing formally for a flight may be long gone, that doesn't mean airport style has to look like pajamas. "Comfort is definitely No. 1 for me, but I still want to look nice!" says Megan Miele, account manager of business travel at Cadence Travel . "My mom was a flight attendant and started flying back in 1969. Back then, you dressed up to the nines to get on an airplane. Flying was more of a privilege and was much more exclusive than it is today.

"Now, almost everyone can afford to fly, and we fly a LOT more often. We also have so many more rules and regulations to deal with. So for me, comfort is definitely the priority, but I still want to feel like I look put together. I'm not trying to show up at the airport looking like I just rolled out of bed," she added.

The modern-day happy medium? Start with pieces you can comfortably sit, stand and sprint to your gate in, then lean on a few smart styling tricks to make your travel look more polished. Layer a chic, cozy sweater over a soft T-shirt and leggings for an easy upgrade, or take the guesswork out of getting dressed with a cute matching set .

Colorfulkoala High-Waisted Tummy-Control Leggings

The best airport outfits include pieces that work smarter, not harder, especially when you're juggling a suitcase, a boarding pass and an overpriced airport coffee. "Layers are useful because airport and aircraft temperatures can vary so much. In colder weather I always take a scarf, which earns its place in my hand luggage several times over: I wear it at the airport and then use it as a blanket, wrap or makeshift pillow on the plane," says McKinlay.

Andrés Serra, trip planner and head of operations at Optimise Travel , has his travel-day formula down to a science. "My favorite travel outfit is a plain T-shirt, elastic-waist travel pants with two zipped pockets, a thin button-up overshirt and low-profile sneakers. The overshirt acts as a light jacket and can be rolled up to support my neck if I need it, and the pants are comfortable for long flights but still look good enough for a restaurant after landing." Cara Laban, founder of TravelReddi , agrees that pockets are a travel-day must. "I recommend pants with large pockets so you can easily grab essentials like your ID or passport and phone without having to dig through your bag," she says.

Choosing travel pieces that pull double duty doesn't just make the journey more comfortable — it also frees up precious space in your suitcase . A button-up can double as a pillow, an oversized scarf becomes an in-flight blanket and a pair of polished pants can hold your essentials and take you straight from a cramped coach seat to dinner without an outfit change. The more versatile each piece is, the less you have to pack.

And don't forget about what's underneath your outfit. Gibson recommends compression socks for long travel days, calling them "a game-changer for leg fatigue and circulation." They may not be the star of your airport look, but your legs could be thanking you by the time you land.

What items help you breeze through airport security?

A little pre-security prep can mean the difference between an easy trip through the checkpoint and becoming that person frantically scooping up loose change and jewelry while the line piles up behind you. "The most useful thing I bring isn't something I wear," says Serra. "It's a small zipped pouch I keep in my personal bag. Before I leave for the airport, I put my watch, coins, wallet, earbuds and other small items inside. TSA suggests putting pocket items in your carry-on instead of leaving valuables loose in a screening tray. This also saves me from scrambling to grab everything while other people are waiting."

Your bag can also do some of the heavy lifting. "If you are traveling with a laptop or iPad, a bag with a separate laptop compartment will make it much easier to get it in and out at security," explains Laban. She also recommends skipping jewelry and belts loaded with metal, since they can add another thing to remove — and another thing to remember on the other side.

And don't forget the right shoes. "If you don't have TSA PreCheck (which I highly recommend), then slip-on shoes, or just shoes that don't have difficult laces, are definitely helpful," Laban adds.

Gibson swears by a crossbody with plenty of pockets, like her go-to Bandolier bag . "It keeps my phone, ID, passport, wallet, headphones and lip gloss within reach. There's even a dedicated front phone pocket, which makes keeping track of everything at security a breeze." Everything should have a designated spot, so you can spend less time digging through your bag at security and more time relaxing in the airport lounge.

articles.title: Why Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in West Bank are pogroms
articles.summary: Waves of settler attacks, aided by Israel’s military, increasingly fit the definition of a pogrom.
articles.body:
Attacks on Palestinian communities by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, which are often supported by Israeli forces, have gathered pace over the past month since settlers from the Havat Gilad settlement attacked Palestinian homes on the eastern edge of Tal, southwest of Nablus.

On Sunday and Monday, the Israeli military raided multiple towns, villages and refugee camps across the occupied territory, and reports of arrests, home searches and settler attacks have continued to mount.

A 15-day siege on three families comprising 15 people, including two children, in the village of Qusra, which is ongoing, drew a rare public condemnation this month from the United States ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, a staunch supporter of Israel and its West Bank settlements.

Israel is also pushing ahead with plans for the so-called E1 settlement expansion close to Jerusalem, which human rights organisations warn would essentially sever the West Bank in two, further hampering the freedom of movement of Palestinians on either side of it and endangering the possibility of a Palestinian state.

The West Bank attacks increasingly fit the definition of a pogrom, experts said. United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories Francesca Albanese described these Israeli attacks against Palestinians as “pogroms against defenceless civilians”.

So why are experts calling settler attacks pogroms, and do they fit the formal definition of one?

Settlers, frequently supported by the Israeli military, have been attacking Palestinian homes, businesses and farmland across the West Bank. Such attacks have been commonplace for decades as settlements have expanded across the territory, but they have gathered pace after October 7, 2023, the day that Hamas-led fighters attacked southern Israel and Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza. The attacks in the West Bank have become particularly violent and frequent over the past month.

Israeli settlements and outposts across the West Bank are illegal under international law.

According to the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, Israeli settlers now number roughly 780,000 across the West Bank and occupied East Jerusalem. They live in 192 settlements and 400 outposts, making up 71 percent of Area C in the West Bank, which is under full Israeli civil and military control, and 91 percent of the Jordan Valley, the commission said.

Settlers often set up outposts without formal approval around Palestinian villages from which they launch a campaign of harassment, including killing and stealing livestock; cutting off water, electricity and supplies; and damaging property to drive local residents out. Once they establish a more formal settlement, they often receive retrospective approval from the Israeli government for the settlement.

In some places more recently, settlers have laid siege to individual family homes, such as in the Ras al-Ein area of Qusra , cutting off water and other supplies and damaging orchards or harming livestock.

This has set a new pattern: Settlers establish a tent adjacent to individual homes; Palestinians’ homes are besieged with essentials cut off; and Israeli soldiers arrive, not to remove the settlers but rather to remove the family – through arrests or for their “protection”.

In Qusra, the three besieged families were forced together into one of the family houses. Meanwhile, Israeli forces have occupied one of the other homes for use as a military post and thrown furniture and belongings from its windows, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recorded more than 1,330 settler-related attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank from January to late July, averaging six a day and marking the fastest pace since the agency began systematic tracking two decades ago.

Separately, a UN-appointed commission of inquiry has found that the Israeli authorities have repeatedly failed to prevent foreseeable settler attacks and, in some cases, have directly enabled them through army protection and the provision of weapons and funding.

OCHA has found that settler attacks, demolitions and evictions forcibly displaced more Palestinians in the first four months of this year than in the whole of 2025.

OCHA reported that 107 communities, comprising 5,900 Palestinians, had been completely or partially displaced as a result of settler violence since January 2023. It also found that the Israeli military has expelled another 32,000 Palestinians from their homes in the West Bank since January 2025, essentially emptying the Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams refugee camps.

Major dictionaries in the US and United Kingdom vary to some degree on the definition.

The British Collins Dictionary identifies a pogrom as “organised, official violence against a group of people for racial or religious reasons” with a notable inclusion of official, or state-backed, violence.

The Oxford Advanced Learner’s Dictionary calls it “the organised killing of large numbers of people, because of their race or religion” without mention of state-sanctioned violence.

Merriam-Webster says it is “an organised massacre of helpless people” – “specifically: such as a massacre of Jews”.

Cambridge Dictionary says it is “an act of organised cruel behaviour or killing that is done to a large group of people because of their race or religion”.

The word is understood to have been introduced via Yiddish and was at first used to describe the wave of violent, organised mob attacks on Jewish communities in the Russian Empire after the assassination of Tsar Alexander II in 1881.

It is important to note that unlike legal terms, including “crimes against humanity” or “genocide”, “pogrom” has no established legal definition under international law.

Can attacks in the West Bank be referred to as pogroms?

Besides UN Special Rapporteur Albanese, who has described Israeli attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank as “pogroms against defenceless civilians”, Israeli officials themselves have described such attacks as “pogroms”.

On February 26, 2023, hundreds of Israeli settlers attacked Huwara and surrounding Palestinian communities after two Israeli settlers were killed. A Palestinian was killed, hundreds were injured, and homes, businesses and cars were burned.

The Israeli military’s then-commander in the West Bank, Yehuda Fuchs, called the settler attacks a “pogrom”, and it was also recorded as such by the US Department of State .

The Israeli-Palestinian human rights group B’Tselem has also previously described Israeli actions in the West Bank as “pogroms”, especially after the February 2023 attacks. Later, it followed up with a report titled, The Pogroms Are Working – the Transfer Is Already Happening, which argued that settler attacks were contributing to the displacement of Palestinian communities.

“Settler violence is not a new phenomenon, but over the past three years, it has become more violent, more systematic and, most importantly, part of a state mechanism intended to ethnically cleanse large parts of the West Bank,” said Yair Dvir, the spokesperson for B’Tselem.

“The government funds and arms the settlers while the Israeli military stands by and, in many cases, actively participates in the attacks,” he told Al Jazeera. “So far, these militias have expelled 64 Palestinian communities and taken control of around 1 million dunams [100,000 hectares/247,100 acres] of land.”

Dvir also told Al Jazeera that the Israeli settlers are “now carrying out organised attacks on established Palestinian villages and towns in order to drive out their residents”.

“These are armed militias operating as an unofficial arm of the state with a shared goal: to ethnically cleanse as much of the West Bank as possible,” he added.

The Lemkin Institute for Genocide Prevention – which is named after Polish Jewish lawyer Raphael Lemkin, who is credited with coining the term genocide after the Holocaust – referred to settler attacks on al-Mughayyir, a Palestinian village in the Ramallah and el-Bireh governorate, as “pogroms”, reporting that hundreds of armed settlers attacked residents and burned buildings and cars while soldiers stood by this year. In 2025, the Israeli military uprooted thousands of Palestinian olive trees in al-Mughayyir.

Raheel Dhattiwala, an Indian scholar who focuses on collective violence, told Al Jazeera: “West Bank attacks fit the characteristics of a pogrom – systematic targeting of one civilian group by another with state approval. A few senior Israeli army officers have called it ‘pogroms’ in the past too, for example after attacks in Huwara.

“One might want to debate the use of the term ‘pogrom’, but it is accurate to call settler violence systematic attacks of occupiers with government approval on groups of occupied people.”

A Palestinian man inspects the damage at a mosque that Palestinians say was damaged by Israeli settlers in Qusra near Nablus in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on July 26, 2026 [Mohamad Torokman/Reuters]

articles.title: Democrats demand Iran war cost details from Trump, Hegseth
articles.summary: Nearly 50 House Democrats reportedly signed a letter to President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asking for more details on the cost of the Iran war. “What was billed as a two-week operation is now a full-scale war that has lasted for over 150 days, cost over $37 billion, and claimed the lives of…
articles.body:
Nearly 50 House Democrats reportedly signed a letter to President Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth asking for more details on the cost of the Iran war .

“What was billed as a two-week operation is now a full-scale war that has lasted for over 150 days, cost over $37 billion, and claimed the lives of 18 servicemembers,” the House Democrats wrote in the letter . “At the same time, prices across the country have gone up significantly, placing the burden of this conflict on American families.”

Democratic Reps. Jason Crow (Colo.), Maggie Goodlander (N.H.) and Derek Tran (Calif.) led the charge on the letter, per NBC. The trio served in the military and co-chair House Democrats’ national security task force.

“The Iranian regime — which for 47 years has chanted ‘Death to America’ and threatened our troops overseas — can never be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon, and the President’s team will continue to communicate with Congress as we work toward this shared goal,” White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told The Hill.

Trump initially said the Iran war would take roughly a month, but the conflict has stretched on for nearly six months without a lasting peace deal between his administration and Iranian leaders. The administration on Monday is ramping up its economic offensive against Iran.

In late July, Hegseth told the Senate Appropriations Committee the conflict had cost roughly $37.5 billion. When reached for comment on the letter from House Democrats, a Pentagon official referred The Hill to that price tag.

But NBC News reported earlier that month the Pentagon’s internal cost estimate of the war was $80 billion to $100 billion when accounting for the costs of repairing damaged military bases, replacing destroyed aircraft and fully replenishing weapons stockpiles.

White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought also asked Congress for $67.1 billion in June for the Pentagon. That included $1.7 billion for readiness, $17.3 billion for operational costs and $21 billion for munitions. The military has depleted its weapons stockpiles during the Middle Eastern conflict.

The war has come with financial costs for Americans, particularly due to the Iranian military’s restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The average price of a gallon of regular gas is roughly $4.09 as of Monday , up from less than $3 two days before the U.S. and Israel launched the conflict, according to AAA.

“It is unconscionable that the Administration is asking for more to fund the very thing that is raising costs for Americans,” the letter from the four dozen lawmakers added, referencing the White House’s supplemental funding request. “The Administration should be focused on ending the conflict and addressing the very real financial concerns of the American public.”

Trump said earlier this month it is worth it for Americans “to pay a tiny, little bit more” for gas so the U.S. military could ensure Iran cannot develop a nuclear weapon.

“So remember that, when you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK. … I’ll never apologize, I did the right thing,” the president said at an event in Garden City, N.Y.

The Democratic lawmakers asked Trump and Hegseth for a “public, comprehensive assessment” of the economic impact of the war by Sept. 11.

That assessment, the representatives noted, should include all Pentagon operational costs, the impact on oil and energy markets and the macroeconomic effects imposed by the war, such as its impact on gross domestic product growth (GDP), inflation and supply chains.

Annual inflation has risen from 2.4 percent in February to 3.4 percent in July , as measured by the consumer price index .

U.S. GDP also increased at an annual rate of 1.5 percent in the second quarter after 2.1 percent growth in the first quarter, based on data released by the Bureau of Economic Analysis .

articles.title: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows
articles.summary: The record "is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress", according to Dr Samantha Burgess from the European Copernicus climate change service.
articles.body:
The world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from human-caused climate change and the growing El Niño weather phenomenon.

The average surface temperature of the planet's seas outside the polar regions hit 21.1C (70F) on Saturday, according to figures from the European Copernicus climate change service.

That edges past the 21.09C recorded in March 2024, and is far above average for the time of year.

Warmer oceans can have wide-reaching consequences, including supercharging extreme weather, raising sea levels and harming marine life.

"This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress," said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus.

"El Niño is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming," she added.

The data is based on sea temperatures 10m (32ft 10in) below the surface, using measurements from buoys, ships and satellites, which are combined to produce a global estimate.

While the margin of record is currently very small and any global estimate comes with uncertainties, scientists say its timing is particularly notable.

Average worldwide sea temperatures tend to reach their yearly peak in March or April, which corresponds to the end of summer in the southern hemisphere - and not in August.

The southern hemisphere contains more of the planet's ocean surface than the northern hemisphere and so exerts a bigger influence on average sea temperatures.

What is especially concerning to scientists is that the oceans are already so hot when the natural El Niño weather phenomenon is still some way off its expected peak.

El Niño brings unusually warm waters to the surface of the eastern and central tropical Pacific Ocean. Warmer waters across such a large area means that global average temperatures typically spike too.

El Niño is expected to keep strengthening until Christmas time, with scientists warning that it is on course to be the strongest in centuries .

This could see ocean temperatures climb yet further.

"The fact that we are already breaking records is an early indicator of how strong the El Niño is becoming," said Dr Jeremy Grist, senior research fellow at the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton.

"All things being equal we might expect the ocean temperature record to be broken again in March [or] April 2027," he added.

The waters far away from El Niño's Pacific hunting ground are also extremely warm, including around the UK and Europe.

The western English Channel has seen almost continuous marine heatwave conditions for more than three years, peaking at 7C above normal in July, according to Prof Tim Smyth, director of science at Plymouth Marine Laboratory.

Scientists say such widespread warmth around the planet is a clear sign of the growing effect that human-caused climate change is having on the world's seas.

The oceans take up more than 90% of the excess heat trapped by humanity's greenhouse gas emissions, mainly from burning fossil fuels.

"The latest Copernicus data reinforce the troubling upward trend in ocean temperatures,” said Smyth.

Warmer seas help to fuel more extreme weather. They can provide storms with extra moisture and energy, and can intensify heatwaves on land in some coastal regions by reducing the cooling effect of sea breezes.

Warmer water also takes up more space, raising sea levels and bringing a greater risk of coastal flooding - while intense ocean heat can be devastating for sea habitats, such as coral reefs.

The increasing frequency of marine heatwaves is already "putting increasing pressure on marine ecosystems and the communities that depend on them", Burgess said.

articles.title: Prince Harry steps down from African Parks charity board
articles.summary: Last year the organisation African Parks  admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.
articles.body:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses against indigenous people.

A spokesman for Prince Harry confirmed he was stepping down after being president for the charity, African Parks, for six years before becoming a member of its board of directors in 2023, but said he remains a "supporter of its mission".

Last year the organisation admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.

Prince Harry's resignation comes shortly after it was announced he was relocating with the Duchess of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet from California to the UK.

Prince Harry's spokesman said "the Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board.

"His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks' mission."

African Parks manages around 20 national parks and protected areas across 12 countries.

It was subject to an independent human rights investigation into allegations guards managed and paid by the charity had beaten, raped and tortured indigenous people in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park.

The charity said in 2025 it had improved its safeguarding processes both in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park and institutionally.

Announcing a "governance refresh of its board of directors", the charity thanked Prince Harry for his association, saying he had "brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa".

It added: "The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks' work."

The charity's website says Prince Harry served as part of the expert team that helped implement the first phase of the 500 Elephants project, which was "one of the largest and most significant elephant translocations in conservation history".

It saw wildlife experts move elephants from a park in Malawi to help increase population in areas where they have been heavily poached.

Prince Harry has said helping move elephants to safer homes was an "amazing" experience.

The Sussexes are back in the spotlight after the revelation last week they were returning to the UK this month after enrolling their children to start at a British school in September.

No change is expected to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.

Their pending return to the UK has raised questions on their security arrangements.

articles.title: Meet Finley Holz, the Minnesota student who studied 10 years of wolf-tracking data and found deep snow can make wolves move less
articles.summary: US News: Holz combined wolf-tracking records with winter weather data, including temperature, snow depth and snowfall. Using ArcGIS Pro, he mapped wolf locatio.
articles.body: Holz combined wolf-tracking records with winter weather data, including temperature, snow depth and snowfall. Using ArcGIS Pro, he mapped wolf locations and converted them into movement data, while a Python programme helped compare movements with weather conditions. His research found that deeper snow was linked to reduced wolf movement. The study recorded a statistically significant negative correlation between snow depth and movement.However, cold snaps did not significantly affect how much the wolves moved. The research also produced an unexpected finding. Wolf movement decreased as a winter storm approached, while three days after a storm, movement was significantly below the average winter level. Holz's project was recognised in a Minnesota Story Map competition, where he placed second.How Finley Holz used wolf-tracking and winter weather data to study wolf movementHolz combined wolf-tracking information with winter weather measurements, including high and low temperatures, snow depth and snowfall events.The project used ArcGIS Pro to organise shapefiles and create maps showing wolf locations. The resulting location points were then converted into movement data. Holz also wrote a Python programme to align the wolf movements with the different winter weather conditions.The data came from wolf collar information provided by the Fond du Lac Resource Management Division. Pine Knot News, a Minnesota-based publication, reports that wildlife programme manager Michael Schrage provided wolf collar data and guidance to the students. Holz and other students also had the opportunity to collar Otter Creek wolf pups on the Fond du Lac Reservation on 5 May.Deep snow was linked to reduced wolf movement in MinnesotaOne of the clearest findings from Holz's research was the relationship between snow depth and wolf movement. According to the project published in Fairfolio, titled âThe Effect of Winter Weather Events on Wolf (Canis lupus) Movement on the Fond du Lac Reservationâ, Holz's second hypothesis was supported: wolves moved less as snow depth increased. The study found a statistically significant negative correlation between snow depth and wolf movement. In simple terms, the data showed that as the snow became deeper, the distance wolves travelled per movement decreased.The finding in similar terms, stating that Holz "found that winter cold snaps have no effect on wolf movement" but that there was "a negative correlation between snow depth and wolf movement: the deeper the snow, the less the wolves moved." Holz had also expected extreme cold to affect wolf movement. His third hypothesis predicted that wolves would move the least during a cold snap. However, the results did not support this idea. The Fairfolio project says there was no difference in wolf movement during a cold snap compared with normal winter movement. That meant that extremely cold periods, at least within the conditions examined in the study, did not produce the reduction in movement Holz had expected.Finley Holz found wolf movement decreased as winter storms approachedAnother unexpected finding came from the relationship between wolf movement and winter storms. Holz originally hypothesised that wolves would travel the furthest immediately after a storm. Instead, the data showed that their movement declined around the time of a storm.According to the project abstract, "Three days after the storm had passed, the wolves moved significantly less than the average winter movement (pFinley Holzâs wolf research earns second place in Minnesota Story Map competitionHolz's wolf research also became part of a successful Minnesota Story Map competition. Two Cloquet High School students and a Hermantown student with Cloquet connections won the top three places in the competition. Hermantown freshman Gabriel Bradley came first, while Cloquet sophomores Finley Holz and Melanie Buhs placed second and third.The Minnesota Alliance for Geographic Education competition challenges students to conduct research and present their findings through an ArcGIS Online story map.Holz's project focused on the effect of winter weather events on wolf movement, while Bradley's project examined factors affecting wolf pack den relocation.Minnesota studentâs decade-long wolf research reveals effects of snow and stormsHolz's project provides a detailed look at how winter conditions can influence wolf movement in northeastern Minnesota. Rather than finding that every form of severe winter weather caused wolves to travel less, the research showed a more specific pattern. Increasing snow depth was associated with reduced wolf movement, while cold snaps alone did not significantly change movement.The study also raised a new question about how wolves respond to approaching storms. The observation that movement decreased before a storm arrived suggests that further research could investigate whether wolves respond to changes in atmospheric or environmental conditions before severe weather reaches the area.For a high-school research project, Holz's work combined a decade of wildlife-tracking information with geographic mapping, weather data and computer analysis to examine the behaviour of an important northern predator.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: This rare polyamorous bird of prey’s location has been kept a mystery. Here’s why
articles.summary: The UK’s rarest bird of prey has successfully bred in a secret location for a second consecutive year, with conservationists crediting one polyamorous male with bringing the species back from near extinction in the country.
articles.body: The UK’s rarest bird of prey has successfully bred in a secret location for a second consecutive year, with conservationists crediting one polyamorous male with bringing the species back from near extinction in the country. Montagu’s harriers – raptors referred to as the “aristocrats of the bird world” – were put on a red list of birds most at risk in the UK in 2021, with no breeding pairs spotted between 2020 and 2023. But one adult male known as AU is now keeping Britain’s “Monties” population alive. He’s responsible for at least 16 chicks since 2018, according to the wildlife conservation charity The Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), including six juveniles that were bred this year with two females in two different nests. AU had previously bred four chicks with a female in 2025, after a six-year wait in the UK for new Montagu’s harrier families. “When we ringed him as a chick in 2016 in a different part of the country we had no idea that ten years later he would single-handedly prop up the species in Britain,” said the RSPB’s Mark Thomas. The charity’s fieldworkers in July fitted one chick from each of the two nests with satellite tracking tags to follow their migration and survival – marking the first time in the UK that juvenile Montagu’s harriers have been tagged. “Monties” travel to Europe from Africa each spring to breed, but only a small number head to the UK, according to the RSPB. AU arrived and began performing his aerial courtship displays in early May, an RSPB spokesperson told CNN. These “acrobatic” displays, known as “skydancing,” feature “high-altitude dives, rhythmic ‘U’-shaped undulations, loops, and twists accompanied by rapid, cackling vocalizations,” the spokesperson said, adding that AU “pulled off the two nests through hard work and a good food supply.” The raptors’ breeding population peaked at around 30 breeding pairs in the mid-1950s, decreasing to zero in 1974, before rising to up to 13 pairs in the late 2000s, according to BTO. A sustained collaboration with farmers and birdwatchers led to breeding success this year and in 2025, said the RSPB, which attributes those gains to keeping the birds’ breeding location under wraps. “This is a sensitive species that is easily disturbed,” the RSPB said, adding that they decided to keep the location of the new nests “a secret” as the birds might also return to the same breeding sites again. Plus, the nests are on private land, they said. One of the two nests spotted this year was found inside a patch of barley left as a habitat by a farmer, with the other nest located less than a mile away, according to the charity.
