articles.title: Terror threat looms over coastal destination as US warns attacks could strike without notice
articles.summary: Terrorists have targeted upscale lodges where international big-game hunters stay in Mozambique's Cabo Delgado Province, the State Department warns.
articles.body: Americans are being warned to avoid parts of an African safari destination where terrorists have targeted upscale lodges frequented by international big-game hunters. Mozambique, a southeastern African country across from the island of Madagascar, is the subject of an Aug. 21 updated "Level 2: Exercise Increased Caution" advisory from the U.S. State Department. Officials have also designated multiple areas "Level 4: Do Not Travel" — citing heightened terrorism risks. AMERICANS WARNED POPULAR TRAVEL ROUTES THIS SUMMER COULD CARRY CRIME AND KIDNAPPING RISKS Bordered by Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, Zimbabwe, South Africa and Eswatini, Mozambique is known for its Indian Ocean coastline, beaches and wildlife reserves. Though not a tourist hot spot, Mozambique draws visitors for its safari tourism. It welcomed over 757,400 foreign guests in 2024, according to government statistics. Cabo Delgado Province, a "Do Not Travel" area, is home to safari and wildlife destinations, including Quirimbas National Park. The State Department also warns that terrorist groups in northern Mozambique are "active" and that there is a risk of terrorist violence and attacks. ROBBERIES, ASSAULTS AND RAPES SPUR NEW US TRAVEL WARNING FOR POPULAR CARIBBEAN GETAWAY "Attackers may strike public areas and tourist destinations with little or no warning, sometimes taking hostages," the advisory says. Alex Perry, an England-based author and veteran foreign correspondent who previously served as a TIME bureau chief, told Fox News Digital the terrorist presence in northern Mozambique is relatively small but particularly brutal. "Mozambique has one of the smaller ISIS groups in the world," Perry said, estimating it has roughly 500 members. "They are spectacularly nasty." Perry, author of the book "Blood Will Flow" about the deadly Islamist insurgency in Mozambique, said militants in Cabo Delgado have carried out mass beheadings, and that the region's tourism industry has suffered as a result of the insurgency. Cabo Delgado has historically attracted a more exclusive clientele, with smaller numbers of wealthy visitors paying high prices for hunting safaris compared with Africa's major mass-market safari destinations, he also said. "They are spectacularly nasty." "This is almost exclusively hunting safaris — people going to shoot animals," Perry said. "That tends to be much smaller numbers of people paying a much higher price." The State Department says Americans who opt to travel to Mozambique are encouraged to enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP). CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Those who must travel to affected areas of Cabo Delgado, Niassa and Nampula provinces are also advised to consider hiring a security firm. "Avoid all but emergency travel between sunset and sunrise," the advisory says, adding that Americans should "keep a low profile." "Have evacuation plans that do not rely on U.S. government assistance. Have travel documents up to date and easily accessible." CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Perry said that, although the advisory highlights serious risks, much of Mozambique remains a beautiful destination for travelers. "On the whole, it's a pretty safe and secure and, as I say, beautiful and enjoyable place to visit," Perry said. "The far north is a dramatic exception." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. State Department for further insights. The warning is one of several travel advisories issued or updated by the State Department in recent months, as officials continue flagging safety concerns for Americans traveling abroad. This month, the State Department issued a Level 2 travel advisory for Ecuador, warning Americans to exercise increased caution due to violent crime, terrorism and kidnapping. articles.title: Charity? Acting? The Cotswolds? What will Harry and Meghan's UK life look like?
articles.summary: The couple's return to the UK is imminent - and what they'll be focusing on here is gradually becoming clearer.
articles.body:
Within the next few days, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex and their two children will have departed California and become residents of the UK.

Since news broke of the move, there has been some confusion as to what British life for Harry and Meghan will look like - but a picture is emerging of the family's priorities.

Over the weekend, there was a deluge of stories about Meghan's return to acting with speculation she would have a role in the next series of The Gentlemen on Netflix, created by British director Guy Ritchie.

Talks are still said to be in the early stages and we understand filming for the third series of the show is imminent - but Netflix has made no comment on who will star, leaving the way open for a former working member of the royal family with an acting background to be cast.

The comedy is about a duke turned drug baron and is mostly filmed in the Cotswolds.

What is clear is that a return to acting more broadly is very much on the agenda for Meghan. It would be financially lucrative for the family in a world of expensive homes, school fees and international travel.

Speaking in June last year to British businesswoman and podcaster Emma Grede, Meghan talked about her Netflix lifestyle series With Love, Meghan, and hinted at a return to acting when asked if she missed that side to her life.

"Sometimes," Meghan replied. "Being back on set with With Love, Meghan was great because I realised how much I miss my crew. I love being around a crew."

But Variety's chief correspondent Marlow Stern says when it comes to deliberations over a potential acting role for Meghan, "a lot of it has to do with scheduling, to be honest".

"They're maybe also negotiating the size of the role and how many days she'll shoot, and also compensation for it. Both sides often play the media to try and push things along, and we could be seeing that."

For Harry, the focus once back in the UK will be on the charity work and patronages he has kept hold of while living thousands of miles away.

He has now completed his final charity engagements in the US before flying back to the UK in the coming days.

In Washington DC, he met military veterans and their families and visited America's main hospital for injured servicemen and women, Walter Reed National Military Medical Centre.

At Arlington National Cemetery, he visited the final resting place of many service personal killed in Iraq and Afghanistan wars where he himself served on two operational tours.

At the grave of Sergeant Michael Verardo, who died last year from complications related to injuries sustained in Afghanistan in 2010, he met Verardo's widow Sarah - who now supports other military families - and their nine-year-old daughter, Elizabeth.

"All my daughter knows about princes or princesses is probably contained to a movie... she whispered to me and said, 'Where is his crown? Did he leave it in the car?'" Sarah said.

"She was very dazzled by the ability to meet him and it made us find bits of sparkle for her at a young age in a very hard experience - and that means a lot to me personally."

It is a reminder of the impact Prince Harry is able to make and what he will hope to bring to an increased amount of public work in the UK.

Plans for a number of charity engagements in September in Britain were already in place.

He will be at the WellChild Awards in London towards the end of the month, continuing his support for the event which honours the bravery of seriously ill children.

There will inevitably be an emphasis on the Invictus Games for wounded service personnel which will be held in Birmingham next July.

In an ideal world, the King, as head of the Armed Forces, would officially open the Games - putting father and son together in public for the first time in several years.

That remains an aspiration from Invictus organisers rather than any definitive plan.

Based in the Cotswolds, settling into school

It's thought the family will base themselves in the Cotswolds. Harry and Meghan previously rented a property there in 2018 and are known to have friends in the area.

Reports that the couple have turned to former Spice Girl Geri Horner and her husband Christian Horner for advice on life in the area have been rejected by Harry and Meghan's official spokesperson.

"Harry and Meghan are great fans of Geri and Christian… the Horners are not advising them on their return, nor have they been asked to do so."

The couple will be back in the UK about a week before the autumn school term begins for their two children, seven-year-old Archie and five-year-old Lilibet. Most terms begin at the end of next week.

It's understood Meghan will concentrate on settling her children into the routine of life in a British school. She is not expected to embark on any kind of full programme of public engagements.

Exploring acting opportunities and running her business, As Ever, will fill her time once her family is settled. She may also appear alongside her husband at some of his charity events.

The couple will keep their multi-million dollar home in Montecito, about a two-hour drive north of Los Angeles. Meghan's mother, Doria Ragland, who has been heavily involved in helping to care for her grandchildren, will remain living in California.

The family is expected to return to the US regularly as well as use the holiday home they have bought near Melides in Portugal.

It is close to a property bought by Princess Eugenie and her husband Jack Brooksbank who have remained close to the Sussexes during the royal fallout.

How involved Harry, Meghan, Archie and Lilibet will be with the wider royal family has not yet been decided.

Over the next few months, several significant royal engagements are in the diary that would involve most senior royals - Remembrance Sunday at the Cenotaph, the Princess of Wales' Carol Service at Westminster Abbey and then Christmas at Sandringham.

Will there be invitations extended to the Sussex family?

Trust remains an issue. There is caution, a degree of wariness and even hostility in some quarters of the Royal Household. These decisions are very much a work in progress.

Harry and Meghan's team has described the move to the UK as being for "an extended period of time".

It is not necessarily a long-term move but may be a chance for the family to experience life in the UK, allowing the children to get to know their grandfather, the King, while they are young enough to not have their education disrupted.

Much of what happens in the months ahead will be a test - of Harry and Meghan's liking for life in the UK, of public reaction to them and of the royal family's ability to continue with their duties alongside the distractions the Sussex family may bring.

The PGSA stated on social media that 45 named vessels have been blacklisted and could have their cargoes confiscated.

“Effective immediately, any vessel cooperating with listed vessels … will be added to the list,” the PGSA wrote on the social platform X, adding that the owners of these vessels can submit a formal application to request their removal from the blacklist.

Some of the ships on the PGSA’s blacklist include several ships owned by the United Arab Emirates’s ADNOC Logistics and Services and Saudi Arabia’s national shipping carrier Bahri, Reuters reported .

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned countries on Monday to cut their financial ties with Iran as the U.S. carries out “Operation Economic Outcast,” marketed as an “economic D-Day,” in reference to the U.S. invasion of Normandy Beach in World War II.

“Well, we are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behavior, why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” Bessent responded to a question about the lack of details about the plan.

Bessent said that President Trump was making calls to world leaders, with the Defense, Treasury and State departments contacting their counterparts with the same warning.

Trump hinted at the “economic D-Day” last week, saying it would be a “CRUSHING” economic operation against Iran.

The PGSA was also targeted, with the Treasury Department sanctioning the new body out of Tehran, one of 60 entities, individuals and vessels related to Iran’s nuclear and missile technology programs and its ability to conduct cyber operations and generate oil revenue.

The Trump administration said its goal in going to war with Iran since Feb. 28 was to prevent it from developing and obtaining a nuclear weapon. Iran has retaliated militarily over the last six months while also shutting down the Strait of Hormuz, where roughly 30 percent of the world’s crude oil is exported.

Iran’s hold over the strait has caused global gas prices and inflation to rise. The national average for gas in the U.S. reached $4.09 per gallon on Monday, nearly $1 more than the average last year, according to data from AAA .

Negotiations to reopen the strait and permanently end the war have stalled after both countries initially signed an interim peace deal in June. After a period last month when both countries exchanged strikes, Trump has vowed to crush Iran through economic warfare.

Bessent hinted Sunday that this economic warfare will usher in a final phase of the conflict.

“We are now entering the endgame. At dawn begins an economic D-Day — the single greatest financial offensive ever marshaled against an adversary,” he wrote on X.

articles.title: Two hours, 500 metres: How Gurgaonâs rain stole my train
articles.summary: Gurgaon rain caused severe waterlogging on Sohna Road, turning a 40-minute trip into a two-hour crawl and making a commuter miss a New Delhi train.
articles.body: GURGAON: I left home in Sector 48 by cab at 1.10pm on Monday to catch a 4.10pm train from New Delhi Railway Station.The plan was to reach the Metro and take Yellow Line to New Delhi. And I thought a three-hour buffer was enough, even by Gurgaon rainy-day standards. I was wrong.The sky had turned cloudy around 11.30am, but the forecast gave no hint of rain. Then, at 12.45pm, it began. By the time my cab arrived at 1.05pm, the roads outside were already waterlogged.Google Maps put the journey to New Delhi Railway Station at one hour 45 minutes â tight, but doable. That estimate meant nothing once we hit Sohna Road.Traffic barely moved. Instead of falling, the ETA kept climbing. After nearly an hour crawling forward, I abandoned the plan to reach the railway station by road and redirected the cab to Millennium City Centre, Yellow Lineâs terminal station, hoping to cover the rest of the distance by Metro. It was barely 6km away, and with the train still two hours off, I thought I had a chance.Gurgaon had other plans.Sohna Road was completely choked. By 3pm, nearly two hours after I had set out, I had covered barely 500 metres, reaching only as far as Subhash Chowk. I turned the cab toward the Metro station anyway, clinging to the hope that I could park and walk in. I couldnât. As 4.10pm came and went, the cab had made it only as far as Sector 47 â nowhere near the Metro, further still from the railway station.The train was gone.Turning back was no easier. Sohna Road remained flooded in stretches, and a journey that should have taken minutes stretched into another ordeal. Sitting in that crawling traffic, one question kept returning: how many others had missed their trains or flights that day, through no fault of their own?There is a difference between missing a train through personal error and missing one because a cityâs roads simply stop functioning after rain. The first is an inconvenience. The second carries a financial cost, a disrupted itinerary and the particular frustration of being stranded by circumstances entirely outside oneâs control.What makes it harder to accept is how familiar it all feels. Every time the city sees heavy rain, the same cycle plays out. Residents flood social media with complaints, authorities promise a waterlogging-free city, officials point to drains being cleared and water being pumped out, and assurances follow that roads will be passable within two or three hours. Then the next spell of rain arrives, and the same roads flood, the same jams return, the same commuters get stranded. Only the promises and explanations change; the experience doesnât.On Monday, I left home three hours before a train that should have taken 40 minutes to reach. Instead, two hours in, I had travelled barely 500 metres. That is not a traffic problem; it is an infrastructure failure that commuters keep paying for, in time, money and disrupted plans.Unless something changes at the root of it, this will not be the last time this city steals someoneâs train or flight after a spell of rain. articles.title: Dollar higher after Iran sanctions, loonie drops after US announces tariff increases
articles.summary: By Chuck Mikolajczak NEW YORK, Aug 24 (Reuters) - The U.S. dollar advanced on Monday, coming off its third weekly decline in four that sent the greenback to...
articles.body:
NEW YORK, Aug 24 (Reuters) - The U.S. dollar advanced on Monday, coming off its third weekly decline in four that sent the greenback to three-month lows after President Donald Trump's administration announced an expansion of sanctions on Iran and separate ‌tariffs on goods from Canada.

The greenback extended gains after U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the expansion of secondary sanctions in hopes ‌they will "sever every economic lifeline" that sustains Iran in the latest effort to pressure Tehran into ending its attacks on ships in the Gulf.

After last week's announcement by the Treasury Department ​that it would double the size of liquidity support buyback operations for longer-dated notes and bonds, CNBC reported earlier on Monday, citing two senior Treasury officials, that Bessent could tap the department's near $1 trillion General Account to help fund bond buybacks, instead of issuing short-term bills.

The dollar briefly pared some gains after the report, along with longer-dated Treasury yields.

"If the reporting is true that the Treasury is going to announce using a slug of its Treasury General Account at the ‌Fed to buy longer-term bonds, it could be an ⁠interesting experiment. Does firing a bazooka at a hurricane work?" said Brian Jacobsen, chief economist at Annex Wealth Management in Menomonee Falls, Wisconsin.

"Lower bond yields at the long end won't fix the debt problem. Longer term, it could make ⁠it worse. The government's debt burden would become even more sensitive to changes in the Fed's policy rate."

The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies, rose 0.17% to 98.99, with the euro down 0.14% at $1.1663.

Long-end yields have been climbing around the globe due to a combination of a solid economic growth outlook, ​expectations ​for rising inflation and concern about swelling sovereign debts, while the Treasury buyback expansion ​to relieve upward pressure on yields has fueled concerns the ‌dollar will weaken as a result.

Trade tensions weighed on the Canadian dollar, which weakened 0.61%, its biggest drop since June 17, versus the greenback to C$1.385 per dollar and was on track to snap a three-day streak of gains, after Washington imposed 50% tariffs on Canadian goods, with Canada promising to retaliate "dollar for dollar" on the new levies.

Trump said in a social media post on Monday that the U.S. will increase tariffs to 50% on all cars, trucks, automotive parts and steel from Canada starting January 1, 2027.

articles.title: A brief history of the RB1 in fantasy football scoring and the dreaded curse that follows the player year-to-year
articles.summary: It's been a tough run for the RB1 in fantasy football the season after their top performance. More from Joel Smyth.
articles.body:
The overall RB1 is the most important player in all of fantasy football. Analyst Joel Smyth goes over the curse of RB1s past, why the overall No. 1 player is so important for winning leagues and who they could be in 2026.

Join or create a Yahoo Fantasy Football league for the 2026 NFL season

Former RB1s of the season prior have not fared well the following season; some would even say they've been cursed. Whether it's injury or a steep decline, the player who dominated the league the year before, often being taken first overall, has failed to live up to expectations in each of the past seven seasons, with Alvin Kamara being the lone top RB exception (although still dipping by 7.0 PPG).

Below is a look at the RB1 from the past seven seasons in Full-PPR formats.

Christian McCaffrey will be up to bat for the third time on this list, with his first two seasons following an RB1 performance ending in season-long injuries that tanked fantasy teams. He's been the overall RB1 three times, making his 1.05 price tag seem plenty worth it, but his three season-killing years make it a terrifying selection at the same time.

To show just how bad the former RB1s have performed going back to 2015, comparing them to the top rookie back is shocking. Over the last 11 seasons, the No. 1 RB selected in the NFL Draft has outscored or performed the same as the former RB1 in PPG in nine of the 11 years. AKA, the Jeremiyah Love counterparts have done better or the same as the McCaffrey counterparts almost every season.

If you can find this year's overall RB1, the benefit cannot be overstated. If you draft the RB1, you win leagues. Last season, McCaffrey on your roster gave you a 25.7% chance of winning it all, up from your average ~8% chance in a 12-team league. Players that come extremely close have similar value as well, with Bijan Robinson being on 27.4% of championship teams because of his Week 17 blow-up. The elite RB upside is the key.

Over the last decade, the difference between the RB1 and an RB1 (the RB12), is incomparable. So much so that even if you combined the overall RB1 with the worst possible RB flex play (the RB36), it would still be more valuable to have than the RB12 + RB13 in nine of the 10 seasons, and not really close with a 4.1 PPG advantage for the RB1 + RB36.

Another great way to show the value gap is just in salary cap leagues. Analyst Justin Boone has Jahmyr Gibbs, the overall RB1 in ADP, valued at $57, while the RB12 Kyren Williams is way down at $24.

Historically, overall RB1s have not been found after Round 2, with only three since 2005 (14%) being selected outside the top-24, with the majority being Round 1 selections. That would narrow us down to 12 RBs.

Gibbs, the current 1.01 in ADP, is my easy selection for the best odds. In short, the Lions averaged over 31 RB fantasy PPG last season, even with an offensive coordinator firing mid-season. The current RB2 is an injured Isiah Pacheco, with Sione Vaki behind him with one touch in 2025. There is a shot he has LT or 2019 CMC-level upside this year.

Robinson and McCaffrey are the next tier behind. McCaffrey has zero issues outside of injury history and age risk, making him a great pick if your league does not have a last-place punishment. Robinson is nearly equal to Gibbs, just on a much lower offense, especially with their current QB room.

Of the later RB picks, there are three other names I think have a good shot. James Cook III is one, with the best combination of offense and offensive line; Cook is only his rumored receiving role away from another career year. Kenneth Walker III has the offense, talent and volume potential to make it happen in Round 2, with an injury scare moving him back in drafts. The goal line and receiving potential as the best offensive skill player on the team makes for a huge opportunity.

Last, I'd give Omarion Hampton a shoutout. If Keaton Mitchell is nothing more than the RB2 he's been in the past, Hampton finds himself in an amazing RB offense with all the goal-line work on a good team. His receiving chops, which we saw in his rookie season, can propel him to the classic second-year ceiling season that we've seen in recent years for players like Robinson, Gibbs, Breece Hall and Jonathan Taylor.
